deep.reconstruction:
Part 1 continues a theorem begun on p. 61.

Theorem (real setting). Let f(x,y) be single-valued. Suppose that for every constant x in an interval I, f(x,·) is a rational function of y. Suppose conversely that for every constant y, f(·,y) is rational in x, and in particular continuous in x. Then f is a rational function R(x,y).

Hilbert's proof, restated:

(i) For each x in I, write the degree of f(x,·) as a pair d(x) = (deg numerator, deg denominator) in N^2. There are only countably many possible values of d, while I is uncountable. So some value d is taken for infinitely many (in fact uncountably many) x. Call this set E_d.

(ii) For x in E_d, write the ansatz f(x,y) = (p_0(x)+...+p_k(x)y^k)/(q_0(x)+...+q_l(x)y^l), with unknown coefficients and a normalization, e.g. q_l = 1 [normalization is mine].

(iii) Pick enough distinct values y_1,...,y_N. Each f(x,y_j) is a rational function of x by hypothesis. The linear system f(x,y_j)·Q(x,y_j) = P(x,y_j), j = 1..N, determines the coefficients uniquely. Cramer's rule then gives each p_i(x) and q_i(x) as a rational function of x. Hence f(x,y) = R(x,y) for all x in E_d and all y, with R rational in two variables.

(iv) Hilbert asserts that E_d is everywhere dense in I. For each fixed y, both f(·,y) and R(·,y) are continuous and agree on a dense set, so f = R everywhere.

Part 2 (after the rule) only opens a new topic: the 'basic problem of reduction', namely to reduce a system of n linear forms a_{i1}x_1+...+a_{in}x_n (i = 1..n) under integral unimodular substitutions of x. The next page continues with Minkowski's theorem that the reduced region in R^{n^2} is convex and bounded by finitely many hyperplanes, and with the volume question for A = det = 1.
errors: Step (iv) has a gap. Uncountability of E_d gives only infinitely (indeed uncountably) many x. It does not give an everywhere dense set: an uncountable set can be nowhere dense, e.g. a Cantor set. A correct argument uses continuity in x for each fixed y to show that the sets E_{<=d} = {x : deg f(x,·) <= d} are closed. Their closedness follows from the vanishing of determinants in the values f(x,y_j), with care about poles. The Baire category theorem then gives an E_{<=d} containing a subinterval. From there one needs a further argument (continuation/identity of rational functions) to cover all of I. Hilbert does not supply this; Baire's theorem dates from 1899.
The ansatz needs a normalization (e.g. reduced form with monic denominator) for the coefficients to be 'eindeutig'. Hilbert leaves this implicit.
Poles: 'f stetig in x for constant y' is false at poles of f(·,y). Continuity must be understood off a finite exceptional set, or in the projective sense.

results.what: A function that is rational in y for each fixed x (in an interval) and rational in x for each fixed y is jointly rational
results.modern_name: Separately rational implies rational (algebraic analogue of Hartogs' separate-analyticity theorem); Baire-category proof
results.usually_credited_to: Polynomial case: F. W. Carroll (Amer. Math. Monthly 1961) and others. Rational/algebraic case: R. Palais, 'Some analogues of Hartogs' theorem in an algebraic setting' (Amer. J. Math. 1978). Earlier folklore is possible.

results.what: Determination of the y-coefficients as rational functions of x by interpolation at finitely many y-values
Statement of the reduction problem for n linear forms under GL_n(Z)
results.modern_name: Minkowski reduction theory of lattice bases / quadratic forms

deep.surprise_reason: A clear 19th-century statement and proof sketch, from a Hilbert notebook (probably 1890s), of 'separately rational implies rational'. That theorem is usually cited from 20th-century papers (Carroll 1961, Palais 1978). The proof uses a pigeonhole-on-uncountable-sets argument that anticipates Baire category, though it is flawed at the density step. It is notable, but it is a sketch with a gap and may have been folklore. The reduction-theory part is only a setup of Minkowski's known theory.

transcription_corrections: The transcription is accurate. 'verschiedne' is Hilbert's spelling. The word 'rationale' is indeed an interlinear insertion above 'Darstellung'. In the last line of the formulas, the subscripts in 'a_{n1}x_1+...+a_{nn}x_n' are correctly read.
